This afternoon


Retrieval augmented generation
Answering from your own documents, with a citation you can open.


Open source models
What you can download and run yourself, and how far behind it is.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Structured and unstructured


Yesterday
Rows, columns, joins. Five spreadsheets and a total you could reconcile.

Everything else a firm holds
Contracts, mail, board papers, policies, reports, decks, notes.


65% of data leaders call their structured data ready for AI. 39% say the same of the unstructured kind, which is most of the volume.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Why not just paste it in
text:
Why not just paste it in


It was not trained on yours
Your contracts were not on the public web. Nothing in the weights knows them.


The window is finite
A million tokens is large and your document store is larger.


You pay for every turn
Input is billed each turn. Pasting the corpus into every question bills the corpus every question.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Four steps


Chunk. Split the documents into passages of a few hundred words.
Embed. Turn each passage into a vector, the same way tokens became vectors on Thursday.
Retrieve. Embed the question and find the handful of passages closest to it.
Paste. Put those passages in the prompt, with the question.



The model never reads your corpus. It reads an excerpt that a similarity search chose.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
A passage becomes 384 numbers

An embedding model reads a passage and returns a fixed-length list of numbers — 384, or 768, or 1,536, depending on the model.

Passages about the same thing land near each other, whatever words they used. “Revenue fell in the third quarter” sits close to “Q3 sales were down”, and a keyword search for “revenue” finds only the first.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Chunking choices







Choice
What it costs




Chunks too small
the passage arrives without the sentence that made it mean something


Chunks too large
the relevant line arrives inside a page of text you paid for


Split mid-table
numbers arrive with no column headings


No overlap
an answer spanning a boundary is never retrieved whole



Split on the document’s own structure — sections, clauses, slides — before falling back on a word count.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two ways to have one


A hosted tool
Upload the folder, ask questions. Somebody else chose the chunking, the embedder and the number of passages retrieved.

A pipeline you own
Your chunking rules, your embedder, your store, and the retrieved text visible before it reaches the model.

Start hosted. Build your own when the answers are wrong and you need to see which passages came back.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Build one over your own documents
text:
Build one over your own documents
Exercise


Put twenty or more of your own documents in a folder — reports, policies, decks, anything real but not confidential.
Have them chunked and embedded into a local store, and have the chunking rule stated in writing.
Add a search tool to an agent, so it retrieves before it answers.
Ask five questions you already know the answers to.
Make it print the passages it retrieved, not just the answer.



An answer you cannot trace back to a passage is not verifiable.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Make it cite, then check the citation
text:
Make it cite, then check the citation

Open each passage it cites and check that the answer is in it.



Ask a question whose answer is in exactly one document.
Ask one whose answer is spread over three.
Ask one whose answer is in none of them, and see whether it says so.



A retriever always returns its closest matches, whether or not any of them are relevant.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Permissions and chunking


The document
Sat in a folder with an access list. Three people could open it.

The chunk in the store
Is a row in a database with a vector next to it. Usually carries no access list at all.

Index everything and the retriever will return a passage from a file the person asking could never have opened.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Retrieved text is untrusted text
Anything that reaches the model reaches it as text, and text from a retrieved passage arrives in the same stream as your question. Whoever can put a document into the index can put instructions in front of the model.

The Sunday morning question: who can write to the corpus, and what can the agent do once it has read one.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: When it is the wrong tool
text:
When it is the wrong tool


Few enough to paste
Twenty pages fit in the window. Retrieval adds a failure mode and buys nothing.


The answer is a number
Totals, counts and rankings come from a query against the data, not a similarity search over prose.


The corpus changes hourly
Every change means re-embedding, and the index is out of date between rebuilds.

Add a document to your index that contradicts another one. Ask the question both answer.
Add one containing an instruction addressed to the agent. Ask an unrelated question.
Ask something answered only by a table you chunked in the middle.
Write down which of the three your setup handled, and what you would change.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What GPQA Diamond measures

Four-way multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by people who hold or are working toward a PhD in the field they wrote for.



25% guessing


34% skilled non-experts, 30+ minutes of open web search


74% PhDs answering inside their own field



Diamond is the hardest 198 of the 448 questions: both expert annotators answered correctly and most non-experts did not. Rein et al., 2023.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
How far behind is it?


Each line is that tier’s best score so far; gray dots are every other model. Source: Epoch AI, 8 Sep 2026.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What Terminal-Bench measures

An agent is given a container, a plain-English objective, and a terminal. It has to do the job: compile the code, train the model, configure the server, find the bug.



7 task domains: software, ML, science, operations, security, hardware, media


4 parts to a task: instruction, container, test suite, reference solution


0 or 1 per task — the tests pass or they do not



Built by the Laude Institute with Stanford researchers. No human baseline is published. The version charted here dates from mid-2025; a harder v4.0 has since cut the frontier to about 60%.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Where each tier stands today

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two numbers, two different answers


The months
Three to five months, on both benchmarks. A model small enough for one consumer GPU is nine to ten months back, on both.

The scores
On graduate science questions the open gap is 3 points. On agentic terminal work it is 33, and the small model solves 23% against the frontier’s 85%.

GPQA Diamond is near its ceiling, which compresses the gap: five months of lag is worth three points because there is nowhere left to go. Terminal-Bench is not near any ceiling, and there the same few months is most of the task.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: What that means for a choice
text:
What that means for a choice


Answer from knowledge
A 27B open model scores 86% on GPQA Diamond against the frontier’s 96%, on hardware you own.


Reason over your documents
A large open model is a few months behind and self-hostable. Test it on your own task before taking the ranking.


Run a multi-step agent
On Terminal-Bench the best open model solves 52% and the best small one 23%, against the frontier’s 85%.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Not every job needs the largest model
text:
Not every job needs the largest model









Where it runs
What it suits




A frontier model
the provider’s API
judgment, long context, code


A mid-size model
the same API, less per token
classification, extraction, routing


A small open model
your own hardware
high volume, or data that cannot leave


A fine-tuned small model
your own hardware
one narrow task, done constantly



The price difference is negligible on a single question and decides the budget at a million classifications.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Distillation, in one paragraph

Run the frontier model on a few thousand examples of your task. Keep the inputs and its outputs. Train a small model on those pairs.

The small model does not become generally capable. It becomes capable at the one task you sampled, at a fraction of the cost per call, on hardware you control.

A version control system tracks every change you make. A commit is a snapshot you can return to.



Install

With a free account, Claude Code pushes your repository to GitHub and pushes later commits when you ask. It uses the GitHub CLI.

Collaboration
Others can clone it, propose changes, and open issues. Working alone, it is backup and deployment.

Mode
What it does

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Permissions in your container
Everything is allowed already, in ~/.claude/settings.json:
"permissions": {
  "allow": ["Bash(*)", "Read(*)", "Write(*)", "Edit(*)",
            "Glob(*)", "Grep(*)", "WebFetch(*)", "WebSearch(*)"],
  "deny": []
}

So nothing prompts you all week. That is a decision about this container — it holds your course files and is reachable only by you — not about how to run an agent on your own machine.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two kinds of instruction

With no instructions of your own, a model answers everyone’s question the same way. Instructions are how that gets changed.



The provider’s
The system prompt ships with the product and is sent on every turn. It regulates behavior: what the assistant is, what it declines, how an answer is formatted.
You do not edit it.


Yours
Added on top. It customizes behavior: how you want work done, what your files hold, the conventions you follow.
You choose what it says and where it applies.

Course Description
Generative AI moved into ordinary business work faster than any recent technology. McKinsey’s global survey found the share of organizations regularly using generative AI in at least one business function rose from roughly a third in 2023 to about two-thirds in early 2024, and to 71 percent by 2025. The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks the narrower question of whether a firm used AI to produce a good or service in the past two weeks, put the national rate at 19.8 percent in May 2026, up from roughly 5 percent in late 2023 and about twice as high in information (39.7 percent) and in finance and insurance (33.9 percent). The gap between those two numbers is itself informative: many people are using these tools, and far fewer organizations have built anything durable around them.
Business uses fall into a few broad categories. There is individual productivity — the drafting, summarizing, analysis, and coding that one person does faster with a model beside them. There is internal deployment — putting a model to work on the firm’s own documents and systems, in workflows that several people depend on. There are customer-facing applications, where the model talks to people outside the firm. And there is the reshaping of the product itself, where AI is what is being sold rather than what makes it. The categories differ less in the technology than in what goes wrong: a bad answer you catch yourself is a nuisance, a bad answer inside a workflow is a process failure, and a bad answer in front of a customer is a liability.
This course covers the first two. We start with individual productivity, because the judgment you need there — knowing what the model is doing, what it is good at, how it fails, and how to check it — is the same judgment every larger deployment rests on. We then move to work that outlives the session you did it in: writing a repeated task down so others can run it, connecting a model to data it was never trained on, generating the document or application someone else opens, and assembling an agent with a deliberately chosen list of things it can do. The course closes on the questions a firm has to answer before switching any of this on — where the data goes, what an outside document can talk the system into doing, and what it costs to run.
The course is hands-on throughout. You work in your own container on the course lab server, and you show what you built to the room.


Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

Work fluently with generative AI in your own tasks — choosing the right tool for the job, directing it well, and verifying what it gives back, with a working understanding of how these models produce their answers and where that mechanism fails.
Turn ad hoc use into something durable — a documented procedure, a connection to your own data, a deliverable someone else opens, or an agent with a defined job — that a colleague can run without you.
Evaluate a proposed deployment on the terms a firm actually decides on: which model and where it runs, what data it touches, what it is permitted to do, and what it costs relative to what it saves.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Tokenization
Text is cut into pieces from a fixed vocabulary before the model sees any of it.
"The cat sat on the mat"  ->  ["The", " cat", " sat", " on", " the", " mat"]

"Unbelievable"            ->  ["Un", "believ", "able"]
Common words stay whole; rare and long words break into pieces. A typical vocabulary runs to about 100,000 tokens.

Numbers break on the same rules, which have nothing to do with arithmetic. 13,963,378.65 reaches the model as a handful of unrelated pieces.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The whole task

Given the tokens so far, predict the token that comes next. That is the entire operation.

Everything a model appears to do — answering, summarizing, writing code, refusing — is that one prediction, repeated.

The input can currently run to about a million tokens, roughly two-thirds of the Harry Potter saga.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Vectors
The model does not work with tokens. It works with numbers.


Each token is a list
“king” becomes 4,096 numbers. “queen” becomes 4,096 numbers that are close to them.
Tokens used in similar contexts end up near each other.


The space is mostly empty
There are far more possible vectors than there are tokens, so most points in the space name nothing.
The prediction can land between tokens.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: A neural network is a function
text:
A neural network is a function


The idea
\(y = 4x\) is a function. The 4 is a parameter.
Change it to 3 and you have the same structure with different behavior.

The scale
Same idea with hundreds of billions of parameters, arranged as a transformer — the architecture published by Google researchers in 2017.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Training


What is learned
The vector for every token, and every parameter in the network.
Both are adjusted together to reduce prediction error on the training text.


What it takes
Trillions of words. Thousands of GPUs for weeks or months. Tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for one run.



Nothing is looked up or stored as fact. The arrangement captures how words are used, which is why it recalls common things reliably and rare things unreliably.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The pipeline


Tokenize the input.
Look up the vector for each token.
Feed the vectors into the network.
The network produces one output vector.
Find which token vectors are closest to it.
Emit a token, append it to the input, and start again at step 1.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Temperature
The network does not output one token. It outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Temperature controls how that distribution is sampled.



Setting
Behavior




Near 0
The highest-probability token every time. Repeatable.


Near 1
Sampled from the distribution. Different each run.


Higher
Low-probability tokens get picked. Text degrades.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
From prediction to conversation
A model trained only to predict the next token continues your text. It does not answer a question.


Role tokens. The text is wrapped in markers: <|user|> your question <|assistant|>.
Instruction tuning. The model is further trained on examples where what follows <|assistant|> is a useful reply.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback. Raters score replies, and the model is trained toward what raters preferred.


The mechanism did not change. What changed is which continuation is the likely one.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Reasoning models
The same trick applied again: train the model to write out its working before it answers.


How it was trained
Reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked — mathematics, code, puzzles — rewarding the chains of tokens that arrived at a correct answer.


Why it helps
The model holds no state between tokens. The intermediate tokens are the only place a partial result can live, so writing them out is the computation.



The thinking you see may be a summary of a much longer chain, and you are charged for the whole chain as output tokens.

An agent has three parts


The model
Decides. Emits text: sometimes an answer, sometimes a request to use a tool.


The harness
Ordinary software wrapped around the model. Runs the tool the model asked for.


The tools
The things that touch files, databases, and other systems.



The model never runs anything itself. It chooses tools to use. The harness executes, and the harness returns information about the tool outcome to the model.

A database or another program.

The loop


You ask. One sentence, in ordinary language.
It picks a tool. The model emits a tool name and arguments instead of an answer.
The harness runs it. Software outside the model checks the call against its rules, then runs it.
The result goes back. The harness appends what it keeps; the model reads it and decides what is next.



Repeated until the model answers instead of asking, or until the harness hits its turn limit.

All of it is text, and the model treats all of it the same way.

Every turn, the harness assembles one block of text:


Fixed each turn
The system prompt. The tool definitions. Any instruction files the harness is coded to include.

Your messages, the model’s replies, and the full output of every tool that has run so far.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Frontend and backend


Frontend
The browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript — it draws the page and collects the clicks.

Backend
A program on a server, listening continuously for requests. Yours will be Python.


You open a URL. The browser sends a request. The server sends back HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser interprets that and shows you a page.


Right-click any page and choose View Page Source. That is the frontend code, exactly as the backend handed it over.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Two kinds of request









What it carries
What the server does




GET
a path, and parameters in the URL
sends back a page, or data


POST
a body — a form, a ticker you typed
whatever it was written to do, then replies




Opening a page is a GET. Clicking submit is usually a POST.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Running it on one machine

The frontend and the backend can be the same computer — your container, or your own laptop with Python on it.



localhost
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The browser asks the machine it is already running on, and the request never reaches a network.


Ports
One machine runs many programs listening at once. The port number tells the operating system which of them gets the request.



You write the app as a .py file. FastAPI is the usual Python library for one, and uvicorn starts it listening: uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000.

text:
Three kinds of tools




Where the code is
Example




Built in
in the harness
read a file, run a command, fetch a page


Yours
a function you wrote
look up a customer in your system


Someone else’s
an MCP server
the Northwind database, EIA, FRED

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
A tool you write
@tool("order_total",
      "Total revenue for one order. Takes an order id.",
      {"order_id": int})
async def order_total(args):
    df = pd.read_excel("northwind_orderdetails.xlsx")
    rows = df[df.OrderID == args["order_id"]]
    total = (rows.UnitPrice * rows.Quantity).sum()
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"${total:,.2f}"}]}
The description is the interface. The model never sees the code.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Tools from an agent SDK

Pre-built code for the harness, and a set of tools that come with it. The Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain.

Read        Write       Edit
Glob        Grep        Bash
WebSearch   WebFetch    Task

The built-ins in the Claude Agent SDK. You choose which to include: tools=[] includes none, and naming a few includes only those.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Where they run







Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep
the agent’s own process — its filesystem, its shell, its network


Internal MCP tools
the same process — whatever it can import, it can run


External MCP tools
someone else’s server — arguments out over HTTP, only the result back


WebSearch
Anthropic’s search backend — titles and URLs, not pages


WebFetch
downloads from your machine, then a small model extracts what was asked




So “on your machine” holds for the filesystem and shell tools. The two web tools are not local: the search runs at Anthropic, and the fetched page is sent there to be read.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Agent options







ClaudeAgentOptions





system_prompt
a string, or a file on disk when it is long


tools
which built-ins to include — tools=[] for none


disallowed_tools
takes a tool out of the model’s context entirely


allowed_tools
the tools that run without prompting


mcp_servers
the servers to connect, plus the one holding your tools


max_turns
how many tool-use round trips before the app stops it




allowed_tools is not a whitelist. A tool left off it still runs — it falls through to permission_mode.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Permission modes, in code







permission_mode





default
prompts before file edits, shell commands, and network requests


acceptEdits
auto-approves edits and common filesystem commands


plan
read-only — proposes changes but makes none


dontAsk
only allowed_tools run; anything else is denied, not prompted


bypassPermissions
everything runs, no checks — sandboxed containers only

Believing it
A wrong number, delivered fluently. Friday morning was this one.


Sending data out
Your material reaching a third party. A contract problem.

An agent doing something on your behalf that you did not ask for. An engineering problem.

What a contract gives you

Enough for

a setting, revocable, data still retained briefly
personal, non-sensitive work

liability, breach notice, audit rights, a subprocessor list
client data, regulated data

the same, covering protected health information
anything under HIPAA

scale and operations

A BAA is required, not advisable. 45 CFR 164.502(e).

SEC Reg S-P
Written policies “reasonably designed to require oversight, including through due diligence and monitoring, of service providers.”

When the contract is not enough


Send less — a schema and a few synthetic rows rather than the table.

A DPA is a promise backed by liability. These three are physical facts about where the data went.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Letting it act

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Prompt injection

The model cannot tell an instruction from a piece of content. Both arrive as text in the same conversation.

Text placed where the agent will read it — an email, a document, a web page, a spreadsheet cell — is read in the same way as text you typed. An attacker needs no credentials, only a way to get words in front of the model.

OWASP has ranked this first among risks to LLM applications since 2025.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
EchoLeak
CVE-2025-32711 · Microsoft 365 Copilot · June 2025


An attacker mails the victim a message containing instructions invisible to a human reader.
The victim asks Copilot to summarize their email. Copilot reads the hidden instructions.
Following them, Copilot places confidential data inside a URL in its response.
The victim’s browser fetches that URL automatically.
The attacker reads the data out of their own server log.


Zero clicks by the victim beyond the summary request.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Three legs


Private data
Something worth taking: client records, financials, an inbox.


Untrusted content
Text an outsider can control: a web page, an email, an uploaded file.


An outbound channel
Any way for text to leave: fetching a URL, sending mail, writing somewhere shared.


All three in one agent is the condition. Remove any one and the attack does not work.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: The question to ask about any deployment
text:
The question to ask about any deployment


The check

Does this agent hold private data, read content an outsider can influence, and have a way to send text out — at the same time?

It is answerable from an architecture diagram, without knowing anything about how the model works.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Blast radius of an Excel add-in
text:
Blast radius of an Excel add-in
The Claude for Excel add-in from Thursday, checked against the three legs.


Private data
The open workbook. With “work across files” on, also the open deck, the open Word document, and the open Outlook email.


Untrusted content
A downloaded template, a vendor file, a data import, or an email from outside.


An outbound channel
Writing into the open document or email, and any connector you have enabled.



“Work across files” is on by default for Pro and Max plans and off by default for Team and Enterprise. Anthropic’s testing found the add-in could be manipulated into extracting sensitive information, modifying data, or taking destructive actions.

text:
Red-team a classmate’s agent
Exercise


Swap agents with someone. You get their code and their tool list.
Diagram it: what private data can it reach, what untrusted text does it read, how could text leave.
Plant an injection in something it will read — a file, a row, a page it fetches.
Try to make it act on the injection. Record what worked and what it refused.
Give the author two changes: one to the prompt, one to the tool list. Say which one you would actually rely on.



Use synthetic data. Nothing in this exercise touches anything real.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Isolation and governance

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Two ways to stop the same thing
text:
Two ways to stop the same thing


Governance
Every call is inspected as it is made and allowed or refused.
Works on the calls you anticipated. Judgment happens at run time, every time.

Isolation
The route does not exist.
Works on calls nobody anticipated. There is nothing to judge at run time.


Real systems use both. The order matters: isolate first, then govern what remains.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Where the call is made from
text:
Where the call is made from

In Claude Cowork, and in most setups a firm will hand you, the machine the agent’s shell runs on has no route to the internet. The connector works anyway.



At the shell
curl https://api.stlouisfed.org/...
Refused. Everything leaving that machine passes a proxy that allows a short list of addresses, and that is not one of them.

Through the connector
fred_get_observations("UNRATE")
Rows come back. Same machine, same model.


Because your machine never places the call. The client end sits outside it, calls FRED itself, and hands the rows back into the conversation. Your key goes with it and is never on the machine.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What each option allows


Open the network instead
Allow the machine to reach stlouisfed.org and it can send anything to any address there, in any form it likes.

Leave it shut, add a connector
It can call run_sql with a SELECT. That is the entire new capability.

The network stays off and the connector goes on.

The connector reaches out from outside the sandbox holding your credentials, so a sentence in a file it reads can ask for that call.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The split


The agent that reads untrusted content gets no private data and no credentials.
The agent that holds private data has no route to the internet.
An orchestrator calls both as tools and never exposes one to the other’s context.


Neither worker ever holds all three legs. That property is a fact about the network and the tool lists, not a rule either agent has been asked to follow.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Your container, as an example



Filesystem
its own — no other student’s files exist inside it


Processes
its own — you cannot see anyone else’s


Network
its own namespace, and it cannot reach a peer container


The gate
your terminal sits behind your own login



Your container is an instance of that pattern.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: A habit, a file, a question
text:
A habit, a file, a question


A habit
Describe the data, require the code, check the counts, reconcile a second way.


A file
A skill, published, that a colleague can install in two commands.


A question
Private data, untrusted content, an outbound channel — asked of anything before it is switched on.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
The Northwind MCP server

A read-only server over the Northwind trading database, at https://northwind-mcp.rice-business.org/mcp.




list_tables
every table in the database


describe_table
column names and types for one table


query_northwind
a read-only SELECT, returned as CSV




query_northwind reads only categories, customers, order_details, orders and products. There is no tool that writes.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Connect it yourself
Add it to Claude Code in one command:
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user \
  northwind https://northwind-mcp.rice-business.org/mcp

claude mcp list shows it connected; /mcp inside Claude lists the three tools. --scope user makes it available from any directory — drop the flag and it lives only in the current project.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Build a data explorer
Exercise


Tell Claude

Using the claude_agent_sdk, create a FastAPI agent app called explorer.py that connects to the Northwind MCP server and allows its three tools. Also create an internal MCP server exposing one tool, run_python, that runs Python for calculations and charts. The system prompt should say the agent is a data analyst for the Northwind trading company, that those tools are its only source of Northwind data, and that it should call list_tables and describe_table before it writes a query. Set tools=[], permission_mode to dontAsk, and max_turns to 15.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Ask it something a chatbot cannot answer
text:
Ask it something a chatbot cannot answer

Which customers ordered in 1997 but not in 1998?



Watch which tools it calls, and in what order.
Check that it described the tables before writing SQL.
Ask for the answer as a chart, and see run_python used instead.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
This morning

Yesterday’s output was a number. This morning it becomes a file or an app somebody else opens.



Creating docs
Excel, Word and PowerPoint out of the machine — including into the template your firm already uses.


Creating apps
How a web app works, then build one and deploy it.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Office files are archives

A .docx, .xlsx or .pptx is a ZIP file containing XML.

Unzip one and the document’s structure, styles and data are readable as text. That is why an agent can edit an existing file in place — keeping its template, its headers and its formatting — instead of rebuilding it.

So “edit the deck the firm already uses” opens the existing file, while “build me a deck like ours” starts from nothing.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Excel that is a model, not a table
text:
Excel that is a model, not a table


A table
Values pasted into cells. Change an assumption and the analysis is rerun somewhere else, by you.

A model
Inputs in labelled cells, formulas referencing them, a chart bound to the range. Change an assumption in the sheet and everything moves.

Ask for formulas rather than values, and name the input cells.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What the recipient opens








Recipient
Format
What it has to carry




An analyst who will extend it
.xlsx with formulas
inputs, formulas, the definition


A manager approving something
.pptx or one page
the number, the chart, the caveat


A job that runs every week
.csv plus a script
reproducibility, not formatting


The record
.docx or PDF
the method, in sentences

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: The deck already has a house style
text:
The deck already has a house style

Asking for “a deck in our style” produces an imitation of the design rather than the firm’s file.

A .pptx template is not a picture of a design. It is a file holding named slide layouts, a theme with the firm’s exact colours and fonts, and placeholder positions measured to the point.

Open one with unzip -l. The layouts are in ppt/slideLayouts/, the palette and typefaces in ppt/theme/theme1.xml.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Fill the template, do not imitate it
text:
Fill the template, do not imitate it


Generating a deck
The model invents a layout. Colours are close. The logo is missing, the footer is wrong, and the title is out of position.

Filling a template
The file is opened, a named layout is chosen, and text goes into the placeholders that layout defines. Everything else is inherited.

Same request, two implementations.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: A skill that knows your template
text:
A skill that knows your template


Put the .pptx in the skill’s folder.
List the layouts by name, and say in prose what each one is for.
Say which placeholder takes what — title, body, source line, page number.
State the rules a human would know: how many bullets before a slide splits, where the source line goes, what never gets edited.




Prompt

Read template.pptx. List every slide layout by name and index, and for each one the placeholders it defines with their type and position. Write that into SKILL.md as a table, then write the instructions for filling it.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: Turn your own template into a skill
text:
Turn your own template into a skill
Exercise


Upload a deck your firm actually uses. Any recent one will do.
Have the layouts and placeholders enumerated, and check the list against what you see in PowerPoint.
Write the skill, with the file in its folder.
Build a three-slide deck from yesterday’s country analysis using it.
Open the result next to a real deck and find what is off.



Some of the firm’s conventions are not in the template file at all.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Build the deliverable
Exercise


Take your corrected country analysis.
Produce it in the format the person who would receive it actually opens.
Put the revenue definition and the row counts on the face of it.
Open the file in the file browser and look at it the way they would.



If you built a workbook, change one input cell and check that the chart moves.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: When a skill is not enough
text:
When a skill is not enough


A skill
For someone who has the agent, the files, and a reason to be at a command line.

An app
For someone with a browser and a question. No install, no terminal, no account.

Same job, different audience.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Frontend and backend


Frontend
The browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript — it draws the page and collects the clicks.

Backend
A program on a server that listens continuously for requests. Yours will be Python.


You open a URL. The browser sends a GET request. The server sends back HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser interprets that and shows you a page.


Right-click any web page and choose View Page Source. That is the frontend code, exactly as the backend handed it over.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Then you click something

A POST request carries data the other way — a form, a country you typed. The server does what it was written to do and replies.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Running locally


localhost
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The browser asks the machine it is already running on, and the request never reaches a network.


Ports
One machine runs many programs listening at once. The port number tells the operating system which of them gets the request.


The app is a .py file that imports FastAPI. uvicorn runs that file and starts it listening on a port.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Three shapes


One page, no server
Everything runs in the browser. A single HTML file you can mail to someone.


A small server
Python behind the page. Needed when there is a database, a key, or a file to write.


A server that calls a model
The page collects a question; the server sends it to the model with your key, not the user’s.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
One page, no server
Exercise


Build a single HTML file that does one useful calculation from your own work.
Open it in the browser from the file browser. No server involved.
Mail it to yourself and open it on your phone.



Nothing to deploy, nothing to pay for, and it works with no network.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
section: A page with Python behind it
text:
A page with Python behind it
Exercise


Take the country analysis. Put a dropdown of countries on a page.
Have the server read the spreadsheets, compute the answer for the country chosen, and return it.
Serve it on port 8000 and open it at your own address on the lab server.
Watch the terminal while you click. Every request appears there.



The terminal prints one line per request: the method, the path, and the status code.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Hand it to your neighbour
Exercise


Give your address to the person next to you and say nothing else.
Watch them use it. Write down every place they hesitate.
Fix the one that cost them the most time.
Swap back and check the fix on their machine, not yours.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text: Deploying an app

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Platform as a service

You hand a host your repository. It builds the app, runs it, and puts it behind a public URL. There is no server for you to administer.

Railway, Render, Koyeb and Heroku all do this. We use Koyeb, which has a free tier.


Create a free account at koyeb.com.
In the control panel, create an API access token. Koyeb shows it once, so copy it then.
Add it to the ~/.env file you made on Thursday, the same way.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
What has to travel


Prompt

My goal is to push this app to GitHub as a new public repo and then create a Koyeb service connected to it. Walk me through it one step at a time.


The host builds only what is in the repository. Data files you told git to ignore never arrive, and the app fails on the host. Nothing from .env belongs in a public repo — secrets go in Koyeb’s environment settings instead.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Put it on the internet
Exercise


Push the app from “A page with Python behind it” to a public GitHub repository.
Create the Koyeb service and watch the build log.
When it fails, read the log before asking. It is almost always a missing file or a missing key.
Open the public URL on your phone, off the lab wifi.
Send the URL to two people in the room.



A custom domain is optional and takes ten minutes: buy one, create an API token at the registrar, and have the DNS record written for you.

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
Deployment, in four lines

What runs on your machine does not run anywhere else until you make it
The repository is the unit of deployment, and it is not the same as your folder
Secrets live in the host’s settings, never in the code
The build log says what went wrong, in order, every time

title: MGMT 803, MBA@Rice, 2026
text:
This afternoon
The app you just deployed answers from what you wrote into it. This afternoon it answers from your own documents instead.
